units.title: Foundations for Functions
units.intro: A **relation** is a set of ordered pairs. Domain = all first components; range = all second. A **function** is a relation where each x has exactly one y. Vertical-line test on a graph: a vertical line hits the curve at most once.

cards.title: 1.1.1 Relations — pairing things up
body: In daily life we pair things all the time: a person with their age, a town with its zoba, a number with a bigger number. Mathematics records each pairing as an **ordered pair** $(x, y)$: the order matters, because "Hagos is the father of Selam" is not the same as "Selam is the father of Hagos".
**A relation** is any set of ordered pairs. We name relations with capital letters $R, S, T, \dots$
- The **domain** of a relation is the set of all **first** elements (the $x$-values, the inputs).
- The **range** of a relation is the set of all **second** elements (the $y$-values, the outputs).
Example: $R = \{(1, 2), (2, 3), (5, 6)\}$ has domain $\{1, 2, 5\}$ and range $\{2, 3, 6\}$. Read the first numbers for the domain, the second numbers for the range — never mix them.

A relation can also be described by a rule, for example $R = \{(x, y) : y = x + 1\}$, read "the set of all pairs $(x, y)$ such that $y = x + 1$". A pair belongs to $R$ exactly when it makes the rule true: $(5, 6)$ belongs because $6 = 5 + 1$; $(3, 5)$ does not because $5 \ne 3 + 1$.

cards.title: Worked example: from a rule to every form
cards.problem: Let $R = \{(x, y) : y = 2x - 1\}$ with domain $\{-2, -1, 0, 1, 2\}$. List $R$ as ordered pairs, give its range and say whether the graph is discrete or continuous.

steps.text: Put each domain value into the rule $y = 2x - 1$: $x = -2 \Rightarrow y = 2(-2) - 1 = -5$.
$x = -1 \Rightarrow y = -3$; $x = 0 \Rightarrow y = -1$; $x = 1 \Rightarrow y = 1$; $x = 2 \Rightarrow y = 3$.
Range = the set of all second elements $= \{-5, -3, -1, 1, 3\}$.

The domain has only 5 separate numbers, so the graph is 5 separate dots: a **discrete** graph. (If the domain were all real numbers, the dots would join into an unbroken line: a **continuous** graph.)

cards.title: Discrete or continuous?
body: **Discrete**: the domain is a list of separate values, so the graph is separate dots — do not join them. **Continuous**: the domain is an interval or all real numbers, so the graph is an unbroken line or curve.

cards.title: 1.1.2 Functions — exactly one output for each input
body: **A function** is a special relation: every element of the domain is paired with **exactly one** element of the range.
How to test a relation given as ordered pairs:
- Look only at the **first** elements.
- If some first element appears twice with **different** second elements, the relation is **not** a function.
- If every first element appears once (or repeats with the same partner), it **is** a function.

In an arrow diagram: a relation is a function when **exactly one arrow leaves each element of the domain**. Two arrows leaving the same $x$ ⇒ not a function. Two arrows **arriving** at the same $y$ is allowed.

Example: $S = \{(-1, 0), (1, 2), (0, 3), (4, 2), (5, 0)\}$ is a function — the outputs 0 and 2 repeat, but no input repeats. $\{(13, 14), (16, 7), (13, 5), (18, 13)\}$ is not a function: the input 13 goes to both 14 and 5.

cards.title: Counting arrows that LEAVE each input
body: Left: every input sends out one arrow (outputs 0 and 2 receive two arrows — that is fine). Right: 13 sends out two arrows, so this relation is not a function.

head: Relation

body: Every function is a relation, but not every relation is a function.

cards.title: Worked example: which relations are functions?

steps.text: $R$: first elements 3, 4, 6, 8 — all different. The repeated output 90 does not matter. $R$ **is a function**.
$T$: first elements 3, 4, 6, 3 — the input 3 appears with 4 and with 9. $T$ is **not** a function.
$W$: input 2 goes to 2 and $-2$; input 6 goes to 8 and $-8$. $W$ is **not** a function.

cards.title: Worked example: which value can x NOT take?
cards.problem: For $R = \{(8, 1), (3, 4), (6, 7), (x, 22)\}$ to be a function, which numbers can $x$ not be?

steps.text: A function cannot pair one input with two different outputs.
If $x = 8$, the input 8 would go to 1 and to 22 — not allowed. Same for $x = 3$ (4 and 22) and $x = 6$ (7 and 22).
Any other value of $x$ is a new input, which is fine.

cards.title: 1.1.3 Graphs of functions — the vertical line test
body: On a graph, two points with the same $x$-value lie on the same **vertical** line. So a graph shows a function exactly when no vertical line meets it twice.
**Vertical line test:** if some vertical line crosses the graph at more than one point, the relation is **not** a function. If every vertical line crosses it at most once, it **is** a function.
Reading domain and range from a graph:
- **Domain**: squash the graph flat onto the $x$-axis — the $x$-values it covers.
- **Range**: squash the graph flat onto the $y$-axis — the $y$-values it covers.
- An arrow at the end of a graph means it continues for ever in that direction; a filled dot is an end point that belongs to the graph; an open dot is an end point that does not.

cards.title: Sweep a vertical line across the graph
body: Left: wherever you place the dashed line it meets the parabola once, so $y = 3 - x^2$ is a function. Right: the line $x = 2$ meets the curve $x = y^2 - 1$ at $(2, \sqrt3)$ and $(2, -\sqrt3)$ — one input, two outputs — not a function.

cards.title: 1.1.4 Function notation f(x)
body: When an equation gives exactly one $y$ for each $x$, we say **$y$ is a function of $x$**. $x$ is the **independent variable** (you choose it); $y$ is the **dependent variable** (it depends on $x$).

To decide whether an equation gives $y$ as a function of $x$, **solve for $y$**: if you get one value of $y$ for each $x$ it is a function; if you get "$\pm$" (two values) it is not. Example: $y + x^2 = 1$ gives $y = 1 - x^2$ (one value) — a function. $y^2 - x^2 = 1$ gives $y = \pm\sqrt{1 + x^2}$ — when $x = 0$, $y = 1$ or $-1$ — not a function.

Functions are named with small letters $f, g, h$. Instead of $y = 4x + 3$ we write $f(x) = 4x + 3$, read "**f of x**". $f(1)$ means "the output when the input is 1": $f(1) = 4(1) + 3 = 7$, so the point $(1, 7)$ is on the graph. Note: $f(x)$ does **not** mean $f$ times $x$.
To evaluate $f(a)$: replace **every** $x$ in the formula by $a$ in brackets, then simplify. Brackets matter with negatives: if $g(x) = x^2 - 4$ then $g(-2) = (-2)^2 - 4 = 0$, not $-2^2 - 4 = -8$.

cards.title: A function is like a machine
body: Put an input $x$ in, the machine follows its rule, one output comes out. For $f(x) = \sqrt{4 - x}$: input 0 gives 2, input 3 gives 1, input $-5$ gives 3. Input 5 jams the machine ($\sqrt{-1}$ is not real), so 5 is not in the domain. The outputs are never negative, so the range is $y \ge 0$.

cards.title: Worked example: a function in real life
cards.problem: A tea shop makes a profit of 0.40 Nakfa on each cup and pays 70 Nakfa rent a month, so the monthly profit is $p = 0.4c - 70$ for $c$ cups. Write it as a function $f$, find the profit for 100 and 300 cups, and give the domain.

Break-even: $0.4c - 70 = 0 \Rightarrow c = 175$ cups.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the domain of the function $$g(x) = \sqrt{x - 4}$$?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Set the restriction under the radical**
For a square root function to yield real numbers, the expression under the radical must be non-negative.
$$x - 4 \ge 0$$

**Step 2: Solve the inequality**
Add $$4$$ to both sides of the inequality:
$$x \ge 4$$

**Step 3: Express in set builder notation**
The set of all real numbers $$x$$ such that $$x$$ is greater than or equal to $$4$$ is written as:
$$\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ge 4\}$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The domain of the function is **$$\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ge 4\}$$**.

**Step 1: Recall the definition of a function**
A relation is a function if and only if each element of the domain maps to exactly one element of the range. This means no two ordered pairs can have the same first coordinate.

**Step 2: Evaluate each option**
- For $$R$$: First elements are $$-1, -4, 1, 8$$. All are unique. This is a function.
- For $$S$$: First elements are $$13, 16, 13, 18$$. The input $$13$$ repeats with different outputs. Not a function.
- For $$T$$: First elements are $$3, 4, 6, 3$$. The input $$3$$ repeats. Not a function.
- For $$W$$: First elements are $$2, 2, 6, 6$$. The inputs $$2$$ and $$6$$ repeat. Not a function.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The correct relation representing a function is **$$R = \{(-1, 2), (-4, 51), (1, 2), (8, -51)\}$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the domain of the function $$h(x) = \frac{x}{x + 1}$$?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify denominator constraints**
For a rational function to be defined, the denominator cannot equal zero.
$$x + 1 \neq 0$$

**Step 2: Solve the inequality**
Subtract $$1$$ from both sides:
$$x \neq -1$$

**Step 3: Formulate domain in set notation**
The domain consists of all real numbers except $$-1$$:
$$\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x \neq -1\}$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The domain of $$h(x)$$ is **$$\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x \neq -1\}$$**.

cards.title: 1.2.1 One-to-one functions
body: A function never sends one input to two outputs. A **one-to-one function** goes further: **no two different inputs share the same output**. Every output comes from exactly one input.

Test with ordered pairs: look at the **second** elements. If an output repeats (with different inputs), the function is **not** one-to-one. $f = \{(2, 1), (4, 5), (-2, -1), (6, 7), (8, 9), (3, 5)\}$ is not one-to-one, because 4 and 3 both go to 5.

**Horizontal line test:** if some horizontal line meets the graph of a function at more than one point, the function is **not** one-to-one. Points on one horizontal line have the same $y$ (output) but different $x$ (inputs).

Test with a formula: find two different inputs with equal outputs to show it is NOT one-to-one (e.g. $f(x) = x^2$: $f(2) = f(-2) = 4$). To show it IS one-to-one, start from $f(a) = f(b)$ and show this forces $a = b$.

cards.title: Sweep a horizontal line across the graph
body: Left: the line $y = 2.5$ meets $y = x^2$ twice (at $x = \pm\sqrt{2.5}$) — two inputs, one output — not one-to-one. Right: every horizontal line meets $y = \frac12 x^3$ once — one-to-one.

cards.title: Two line tests, two different questions
body: Vertical line test → "is this graph a function?" (one output for each input). Horizontal line test → "is this function one-to-one?" (one input for each output). Do the vertical test first; the horizontal test only makes sense for a function.

cards.title: Worked example: showing a function is NOT one-to-one
cards.problem: Is $f(x) = \frac{3}{x^2 + 1}$ one-to-one?

steps.text: Look for two different inputs with the same output. Because of $x^2$, try $x = 1$ and $x = -1$.
Two different inputs, same output ⇒ not one-to-one.

cards.title: Worked example: proving a function IS one-to-one
cards.problem: Show that $f(x) = 5x - \frac12$ is one-to-one.

steps.text: Suppose two inputs $a$ and $b$ give the same output: $f(a) = f(b)$.
Then $5a - \frac12 = 5b - \frac12$.
Add $\frac12$: $5a = 5b$. Divide by 5: $a = b$.
Equal outputs force equal inputs, so no two different inputs share an output.

cards.answer: Yes — every linear function $f(x) = mx + b$ with $m \ne 0$ is one-to-one.

cards.title: 1.2.2 Inverse of a relation and of a function
body: The **inverse** of a relation $R$, written $R^{-1}$, is obtained by **swapping the two entries of every ordered pair**. If $R = \{(1, 3), (2, 5), (3, 7)\}$ then $R^{-1} = \{(3, 1), (5, 2), (7, 3)\}$.
Because the entries swap, the **domain of $R^{-1}$ is the range of $R$**, and the **range of $R^{-1}$ is the domain of $R$**.
The inverse of a function is **not always** a function. $g = \{(3, 6), (8, 6)\}$ gives $g^{-1} = \{(6, 3), (6, 8)\}$ — input 6 has two outputs. This happens exactly when $g$ is not one-to-one.
**Key fact:** the inverse of a function $f$ is a function **if and only if $f$ is one-to-one**. Then we write it $f^{-1}$ (read "f inverse"). Careful: $f^{-1}(x)$ does **not** mean $\frac{1}{f(x)}$.

cards.title: The inverse reverses every arrow
body: $f = \{(-1, 2), (-3, 1), (0, -2), (5, 6)\}$ is one-to-one, so reversing the arrows still leaves one arrow from each input: $f^{-1} = \{(2, -1), (1, -3), (-2, 0), (6, 5)\}$ is a function.

cards.title: Four steps to the formula of an inverse
body: **Step 1.** Replace $f(x)$ by $y$.
**Step 2.** Interchange $x$ and $y$.
**Step 3.** Solve the new equation for $y$.
**Step 4.** Replace $y$ by $f^{-1}(x)$ — and state its domain (= the range of $f$).
Check: $f(f^{-1}(x)) = x$ and $f^{-1}(f(x)) = x$. Quick number check: if $f(2) = 7$ then $f^{-1}(7)$ must be 2.

cards.title: Worked example: inverse of a linear function
cards.problem: Find $f^{-1}(x)$ for $f(x) = 3x - 6$.

steps.text: Replace $f(x)$ by $y$: $y = 3x - 6$.
Swap $x$ and $y$: $x = 3y - 6$.
Solve for $y$: $x + 6 = 3y \Rightarrow y = \frac{x + 6}{3} = \frac13 x + 2$.

cards.title: Worked example: inverse of a rational function
cards.problem: Find $g^{-1}(x)$ for $g(x) = \frac{x - 2}{x + 3}$.

steps.text: $y = \frac{x - 2}{x + 3}$; swap: $x = \frac{y - 2}{y + 3}$.
Multiply both sides by $(y + 3)$: $xy + 3x = y - 2$.
Collect the $y$ terms on one side: $xy - y = -3x - 2$.
Factor out $y$: $y(x - 1) = -3x - 2$, so $y = \frac{-3x - 2}{x - 1} = \frac{3x + 2}{1 - x}$.
Domain of $g^{-1}$: $x \ne 1$ (that is exactly the value $g$ never reaches).

cards.title: Worked example: inverse with a cube and with a square root
cards.problem: Find the inverses of (a) $h(x) = x^3 + 3$ and (b) $k(x) = \sqrt{x - 1}$.

steps.text: (a) $x = y^3 + 3 \Rightarrow y^3 = x - 3 \Rightarrow y = \sqrt[3]{x - 3}$. So $h^{-1}(x) = \sqrt[3]{x - 3}$ for all real $x$.
(b) $k$ has domain $x \ge 1$ and range $y \ge 0$. Swap: $x = \sqrt{y - 1}$.
Square both sides: $x^2 = y - 1 \Rightarrow y = x^2 + 1$.
The domain of $k^{-1}$ is the range of $k$, so $k^{-1}(x) = x^2 + 1$ **for $x \ge 0$ only**.

cards.title: Worked example: Celsius and Fahrenheit
cards.problem: Water freezes at 0 °C = 32 °F and boils at 100 °C = 212 °F, and Celsius $y$ is a linear function of Fahrenheit $x$. Find the formula, its inverse, and convert 50 °F and 20 °C.

steps.text: Inverse: swap, $x = \frac59(y - 32) \Rightarrow y - 32 = \frac95 x \Rightarrow C^{-1}(x) = \frac95 x + 32$.

cards.title: Worked example: find and check an inverse
cards.problem: Find the inverse of f(x) = (3x − 2)/5 and check it.

steps.text: Step 1: write y = (3x − 2)/5.
Step 2: swap x and y: x = (3y − 2)/5.
Step 3: solve for y: 5x = 3y − 2 → 3y = 5x + 2 → y = (5x + 2)/3.
Step 4: rename: f⁻¹(x) = (5x + 2)/3.
Step 5: check with a number: f(4) = (12 − 2)/5 = 2 and f⁻¹(2) = (10 + 2)/3 = 4 ✔.

cards.title: Tip
body: To find an inverse: replace f(x) with y, swap, solve, rename. Then check f(f⁻¹(x))=x on the new domain.

cards.title: 1.2.3 Graph of the inverse — a mirror in y = x
body: Swapping the coordinates of a point $(a, b)$ gives $(b, a)$. On squared paper with equal scales, $(b, a)$ is the **mirror image of $(a, b)$ in the line $y = x$** — fold the paper along $y = x$ and the two points land on each other.
So the **graph of $f^{-1}$ is the reflection of the graph of $f$ in the line $y = x$.** To draw it: plot a few points of $f$, swap their coordinates, plot those, and join them.
Points that lie on $y = x$ itself stay where they are, so $f$ and $f^{-1}$ meet on the line $y = x$ (if they meet at all).
Always use the **same scale on both axes**, otherwise the mirror picture is distorted.

cards.title: Swap the coordinates = reflect in y = x
body: $(3, 1) \leftrightarrow (1, 3)$, $(-2, 0) \leftrightarrow (0, -2)$, $(-1, 2) \leftrightarrow (2, -1)$. The dashed segment joining each pair is cut at right angles and in half by the line $y = x$.

cards.title: f(x) = 2x + 1 and its inverse
body: From $y = 2x + 1$: swap and solve, $x = 2y + 1 \Rightarrow f^{-1}(x) = \frac{x - 1}{2}$. The point $(1, 3)$ on $f$ becomes $(3, 1)$ on $f^{-1}$. Both lines cross $y = x$ at $(-1, -1)$. Slopes 2 and $\frac12$ are reciprocals — true for every linear function and its inverse.

cards.title: A curve and its inverse
body: $f(x) = x^2$ is not one-to-one on all real numbers, but if we keep only $x \ge 0$ it is. Its inverse is $f^{-1}(x) = \sqrt{x}$; $(2, 4)$ on $f$ matches $(4, 2)$ on $f^{-1}$.

units.title: Geometric Structure
units.intro:
Geometry here is an **axiomatic system**: undefined terms (point, line, plane), definitions, axioms/postulates you accept, then theorems you prove. A conjecture is a guess with reasons; a proof is a chain that forces the guess.

Attributes: sides, angles, parallel, perpendicular, convex, regular. Know the difference between a drawing (picture) and a figure defined by marks (tick equal sides, arrow parallel).

cards.title: 2.1 Why geometry starts with undefined terms
body: Try to define a square: "a quadrilateral with four equal sides and four right angles". Then define *side* ("a line segment"), then *segment* ("two points and all points between them"), then *point*… Sooner or later you go round in circles. To stop this, geometry **chooses a few simple words that are not defined**: **point, line and plane**. Everything else is built from them.
- **Point**: an exact position. It has no length, width or thickness. Drawn as a dot, named with a capital letter ($A$), or by coordinates $(x, y)$ on the plane.
- **Line**: straight, no thickness, goes on for ever in both directions (drawn with two arrowheads). Named by a small letter ($l$, $h$) or two of its points ($\overleftrightarrow{AB}$).

- **Plane**: a flat surface with no thickness that goes on for ever in all directions. Drawn like a table top (a parallelogram) and named with a letter ($m$) — the drawing has edges, the plane does not.
Real objects only *model* these ideas: the tip of a needle or a corner of a box ≈ point; the edge of a table ≈ line; the floor or a TV screen ≈ plane.

cards.title: Definitions are built from undefined terms
body: A **definition** gives the exact meaning of a new word using undefined terms and words defined earlier. A good definition is short, precise and can be read both ways ("if… then…" and "only if").
- **Collinear points** are points that lie on the same line.
- **Coplanar points** are points that lie in the same plane.
- A **line segment** $\overline{AB}$ is the points $A$ and $B$ and all the points of the line between them.
- A **ray** $\overrightarrow{AB}$ starts at $A$ and goes on for ever through $B$.
- An **angle** is two rays with a common end point (the **vertex**).
"A line is a set of points" is a poor definition: a circle is also a set of points. It does not say which points.

cards.title: Axioms (postulates) and theorems
body: Just as we cannot define every word, we cannot **prove** every statement — a proof must start somewhere. So we accept a few basic statements **without proof**. These are **axioms** or **postulates**. Statements that we **prove** from axioms, definitions and earlier theorems are **theorems**.
Postulates about points, lines and planes:
- **P1.** A line contains at least two points; a plane contains at least three non-collinear points.
- **P2.** Through any two points there is **exactly one** line.
- **P3.** Through any three non-collinear points there is **exactly one** plane.
- **P4.** If two planes intersect, their intersection is a line.

Other familiar axioms (common notions): things equal to the same thing are equal to each other; the whole is greater than the part; the shortest path between two points is the straight segment joining them.

cards.title: Postulates P2 and P3
body: Why a three-legged stool never wobbles: its three feet are three non-collinear points, and they fix exactly one plane — the floor.

cards.title: Worked example: theorem or axiom?
cards.problem: Sort into axioms and theorems: (a) the whole is greater than the part; (b) an exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles; (c) things equal to the same thing are equal to each other; (d) in an isosceles triangle the line from the vertex to the midpoint of the base is perpendicular to the base.

steps.text: Ask: "is this so basic that we simply accept it, or can it be shown from simpler facts?"
(a) and (c) are obvious common notions, accepted without proof → **axioms**.
(b) follows from the angle sum of a triangle and a straight angle → **theorem** (proved in 2.4).
(d) follows from congruent triangles (SSS) → **theorem**.

cards.q: Which of the following represents the complete set of undefined terms in Euclidean geometry?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define undefined terms**
In geometry, we cannot define every term without creating circular arguments. Therefore, we establish a starting baseline of terms that are accepted without formal definition.

**Step 2: Identify the baseline terms**
The three fundamental undefined terms that serve as the building blocks for all other geometric definitions are Point, Line, and Plane.

**Step 3: Evaluate other options**
Segments, angles, and polygons are all defined terms built from points, lines, and planes.

**Step 4: Final Result**
The complete set is **Point, Line, Plane**.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand the definition of a Postulate**
A Postulate (or Axiom) is a statement that is accepted as true without proof, serving as a starting point for geometric reasoning.

**Step 2: Evaluate the options**
- "Through any two points there is exactly one line" is accepted as true without proof. It is Euclid's First Postulate.
- "Vertically opposite angles are equal" is a theorem that must be proven logically.
- "The sum of the interior angles of a triangle is $$180^{\circ}$$" is a theorem (proven using parallel lines).
- "An exterior angle..." is also a proven theorem.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The statement that is a postulate is **Through any two points there is exactly one line.**

**Step 3:** Theorems are statements proved from the axioms; corollaries follow directly from theorems.

**Tip:** "Point", "line" and "plane" are undefined terms in Euclidean geometry.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: Which of the following represents the complete set of undefined terms in Euclidean geometry?

steps.text: **Step 1: Define undefined terms**
In geometry, we cannot define every term without creating circular arguments. Therefore, we establish a starting baseline of terms that are accepted without formal definition.
**Step 2: Identify the baseline terms**
The three fundamental undefined terms that serve as the building blocks for all other geometric definitions are Point, Line, and Plane.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: Which of the following statements is a Postulate (Axiom) in geometry?

steps.text: **Step 1: Understand the definition of a Postulate**
A Postulate (or Axiom) is a statement that is accepted as true without proof, serving as a starting point for geometric reasoning.
**Step 2: Evaluate the options**
- "Through any two points there is exactly one line" is accepted as true without proof. It is Euclid's First Postulate.

cards.answer: Through any two points there is exactly one line.

cards.title: 2.2 Attributes of figures and constructions
body: Geometric figures are described by their **attributes**: the number of sides, the lengths of the sides, the sizes of the angles, which sides are parallel or perpendicular, what the diagonals do, and so on. A square, for example, has 4 equal sides, 4 right angles, 2 pairs of parallel sides and equal diagonals that bisect each other at right angles.

A **construction** is an accurate drawing made with only two tools: a **straightedge** (a ruler without marks, for straight lines) and a **compass** (for circles and arcs). We do not measure with a ruler scale or a protractor — the compass copies lengths for us.
Why this works: every point on an arc is the same distance (the radius) from the centre. So two arcs of the same radius transfer a length exactly.

steps.text: Draw a ray and mark its end point $R$ — the new segment will start here.
Put the compass point on $P$ and open it until the pencil is on $Q$. The compass width is now $PQ$.
Without changing the width, put the point on $R$ and draw an arc across the ray.
Call the crossing point $S$. Then $RS = PQ$, because both are radii of the same compass setting.

cards.title: Construction 2: bisect a segment AB (find its midpoint)

steps.text: Open the compass to more than half of $AB$ (using $AB$ itself is easy). With centre $A$ draw arcs above and below the segment.
With the **same** width and centre $B$ draw arcs that cross the first ones.
Name the crossing points $P$ and $Q$ and join them with the straightedge.
$PQ$ cuts $AB$ at its midpoint $M$, and at right angles: $PQ$ is the **perpendicular bisector** of $AB$. ($P$ and $Q$ are each the same distance from $A$ and $B$.)
Draw a ray with end point $D$.
With centre $A$ draw an arc cutting both arms at $B$ and $C$. With the same width and centre $D$ draw a long arc cutting the ray at $E$.
Set the compass to the distance $BC$. With centre $E$ draw an arc crossing the long arc at $F$.
Draw ray $DF$. Then $\angle EDF = \angle BAC$ (triangles $ABC$ and $DEF$ have three equal sides).
With centre $P$ draw an arc cutting both arms at $Q$ and $R$.
With centre $Q$ draw an arc inside the angle.
With the same width and centre $R$ draw an arc crossing it at $W$.
Draw ray $PW$: it is the **angle bisector** — here a 60° angle is cut into two 30° angles.

Key idea

cards.title: Polygons inscribed in a circle
body: A polygon is **inscribed** in a circle when **every vertex lies on the circle**. Any points on the circle, joined in order, give an inscribed polygon.

A **regular** inscribed polygon (all sides equal) with $n$ sides: divide the full turn $360°$ by $n$ to get the angle at the centre, $\frac{360°}{n}$. Mark that angle again and again from a radius; the points on the circle are the vertices.
- Hexagon: $360° \div 6 = 60°$. Each central triangle is equilateral, so **each side equals the radius** — you can step the compass (set to the radius) six times round the circle.
- Square: $360° \div 4 = 90°$: draw two perpendicular diameters.
- Octagon: $360° \div 8 = 45°$: bisect the right angles of the square.
For an inscribed **rectangle**, the diagonals are diameters, so the centre is where the diagonals cross.

cards.title: Regular hexagon: step the radius six times
Rectangle 8 × 6 inscribed in a circle
body: The diagonal is a diameter: $d = \sqrt{8^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{100} = 10$, so the radius is $5$ and the centre is the crossing point of the diagonals.

cards.title: Worked example: the side of a square inscribed in a circle
cards.problem: A square $ABCD$ is inscribed in a circle of radius 3 cm. Find the length of one side.

steps.text: The diagonals of the square are diameters: $AC = 2 \times 3 = 6$ cm.
Triangle $ABC$ has a right angle at $B$ and $AB = BC = s$. By Pythagoras $s^2 + s^2 = 6^2$.
$2s^2 = 36 \Rightarrow s^2 = 18 \Rightarrow s = \sqrt{18} = 3\sqrt2 \approx 4.24$ cm.

cards.title: Worked example: using attributes
cards.problem: In parallelogram ABCD, ∠A = 3x + 10 and ∠B = 2x + 20. Find all four angles.

steps.text: Step 1: consecutive angles of a parallelogram are co-interior angles between parallel sides, so ∠A + ∠B = 180°.
Step 4: opposite angles are equal: ∠C = ∠A = 100°, ∠D = ∠B = 80°. Check: 100 + 80 + 100 + 80 = 360° ✔.

cards.title: Worked example: segments from given segments
cards.problem: $AB = 3$ cm and $CD = 2$ cm. Describe how to construct segments of length $AB + CD$ and $2AB + CD$ with compass and straightedge only.

steps.text: Draw a long ray from a point $X$.
Set the compass to $AB$; from $X$ cut the ray at $Y$: $XY = 3$ cm.
Set the compass to $CD$; from $Y$ cut the ray further at $Z$: $XZ = AB + CD = 5$ cm.
For $2AB + CD$: step $AB$ twice from $X$ (to $Y$, then to $Y'$), then step $CD$ once: total $3 + 3 + 2 = 8$ cm.

cards.answer: Lay the copied lengths end to end along one ray.

cards.q: Which quadrilateral always has diagonals that are equal AND perpendicular?
cards.why: A rectangle has equal diagonals; a rhombus has perpendicular diagonals; only the square (which is both a rectangle and a rhombus) always has both properties.

cards.title: Practice
cards.q: Two angles are supplementary and one is 4 times the other. What is the smaller angle?
cards.why: x + 4x = 180°, so 5x = 180° and x = 36° (the other is 144°). 18° would be for complementary angles (sum 90°).

cards.q: An isosceles triangle has a vertex angle of 40°. What is each base angle?
cards.why: The base angles are equal and the angles sum to 180°: 2b + 40° = 180°, so b = 70°.

cards.title: 2.3 Conjectures — educated guesses from patterns
body: A **conjecture** is a statement that **seems** true because of what we observed in drawings, measurements or examples, but which has **not been proved yet**. Making conjectures is how new mathematics is discovered.
How to make a conjecture: (1) draw or calculate several cases; (2) record the results in a table; (3) look for what stays the same; (4) state it as a general sentence.
Examples from drawings:
- Two intersecting lines: the opposite angles always measure the same → conjecture "**vertically opposite angles are equal**".
- Parallel lines and a transversal: the alternate interior angles always match → "**alternate angles are equal**".
- Measure the angles of many triangles: the total is always about $180°$ → "**the angles of a triangle add up to $180°$**".

A conjecture can be **false**. Measurements are never exact, and a pattern can break later. One **counter-example** is enough to show a conjecture is false; but no number of examples proves it true — only a proof does.

cards.title: Conjecture: vertically opposite angles are equal
body: Lines $AC$ and $BD$ cross at $O$. The angles marked $x$ face each other; so do the angles marked $y$. Measure them: they match. In 2.4 we prove it.

cards.title: Conjecture: alternate angles are equal
body: Line $m$ cuts the parallel lines $h$ and $k$. The alternate interior angles 1 and 2 (a "Z" shape) are equal; the corresponding angles 3 and 4 (an "F" shape) are equal; co-interior angles such as 1 and 4 (a "C" shape) add up to $180°$.

cards.title: Proof habit
body: Given → diagram with marks → state a known fact (vertically opposite, alternate angles, SAS…) → conclude. One reason per line.

cards.title: Worked example: making a conjecture from a table
cards.problem: A circle is cut by lines through its centre. 1 line gives 2 regions, 2 lines give 4, 3 lines give 6. Make a conjecture for $n$ lines and use it for 5 and 8 lines.

steps.text: Table: $n$ = 1, 2, 3 → regions 2, 4, 6.
Each new line through the centre adds 2 regions (it cuts two old regions in half).
Conjecture: $n$ lines through the centre give $2n$ regions.
For 5 lines: $2 \times 5 = 10$; for 8 lines: $16$ regions. (Check one by drawing — 4 lines give 8.)

cards.title: Worked example: disprove with a counter-example
cards.problem: Conjecture: "For every whole number n, n² + n + 41 is a prime number." Is it true?

steps.text: Step 1: test small values: n = 0 → 41, n = 1 → 43, n = 2 → 47 — all prime. The pattern looks convincing.
Step 2: try a clever value: n = 41 gives 41² + 41 + 41 = 41(41 + 1 + 1) = 41 × 43.
Step 3: 41 × 43 = 1763 has factors 41 and 43, so it is not prime.
Step 4: one counter-example disproves the conjecture.

cards.title: Worked example: a conjecture that breaks
cards.problem: Points are put on a circle and every pair is joined. 2 points → 2 regions, 3 → 4, 4 → 8, 5 → 16. Conjecture: $n$ points give $2^{n-1}$ regions. Is it true?

steps.text: The pattern 2, 4, 8, 16 suggests doubling, so 6 points should give 32 regions.
Draw it carefully (points not evenly spaced so that no three chords meet at one point): you get only **31** regions.
One counter-example is enough: the conjecture is **false**, even though it worked four times.

cards.title: Tip: verification is not proof
body: Checking examples (3 + 5 = 8, 7 + 9 = 16…) **verifies** a conjecture for those numbers only. A **proof** must work for every case — usually by using letters, e.g. odd numbers $2m + 1$ and $2n + 1$.

cards.title: More notes
body: You cannot prove an axiom; you use it. “Two points determine a line” is that kind of start. A counter-example kills a conjecture (one drawing is enough). Do not argue from an inaccurate sketch — mark what is given, not what “looks” equal.

cards.title: Practice
cards.q: Which is a counter-example to "If a number is divisible by 2, it is divisible by 4"?
cards.why: A counter-example must make the "if" part true and the "then" part false. 6 is divisible by 2 but not by 4. 8 and 12 satisfy both parts; 7 does not satisfy the "if" part.

cards.title: Practice
cards.q: Reaching a general conclusion from observed examples is called…
cards.why: Inductive reasoning goes from examples to a general conjecture. Deductive reasoning goes from accepted statements to a certain conclusion (a proof).

cards.title: Practice
cards.q: How many examples are needed to show that a conjecture is false?
cards.why: A general statement claims something for every case, so a single case where it fails is enough to disprove it.

cards.title: 2.4 Inductive and deductive reasoning
body: **Inductive reasoning** goes from several particular cases to a general conclusion (a conjecture). Example: the angles of the five triangles I drew add up to about $180°$, so every triangle probably has angle sum $180°$. It is useful for discovering, but the conclusion **may be false**.

**Deductive reasoning** goes from accepted general statements (definitions, axioms, proved theorems) to a conclusion that **must** be true. Example: "All mammals are warm-blooded. A cow is a mammal. Therefore a cow is warm-blooded."
The deductive pattern: **If $p$ then $q$. $p$ is true. Therefore $q$ is true.** ("All rectangles are parallelograms; $ABCD$ is a rectangle; so $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.")

A **proof** is a chain of deductive steps, each justified by a reason (given, definition, axiom or earlier theorem), that leads from the hypothesis to the conclusion. Once a conjecture is proved it becomes a **theorem**.

Deductive

cards.title: Conditional statements and converses
body: Most theorems are **conditional statements**: "**If** $p$, **then** $q$." The part after *if* ($p$) is the **hypothesis** (what is given); the part after *then* ($q$) is the **conclusion** (what must be proved).
The **converse** swaps them: "If $q$, then $p$." A true statement can have a **false** converse:
- "If a figure is a triangle, then it is a polygon." — true.
- Converse: "If a figure is a polygon, then it is a triangle." — false (a square is a polygon but not a triangle).
When a statement and its converse are both true we can join them with "**if and only if**": "A triangle is equilateral if and only if all its angles are $60°$."

cards.title: Why the converse can fail
body: The triangles sit inside the polygons. So "triangle ⇒ polygon" is true, but a square is a polygon outside the triangles, so "polygon ⇒ triangle" is false.

cards.title: Proof: vertically opposite angles are equal
cards.problem: Lines $AB$ and $CD$ meet at $O$. Prove that $\angle AOD = \angle COB$.

steps.text: $\angle AOD + \angle DOB = 180°$ — reason: $AOB$ is a straight angle.
$\angle COB + \angle BOD = 180°$ — reason: $COD$ is a straight angle.
So $\angle AOD + \angle DOB = \angle COB + \angle DOB$ — reason: things equal to the same thing ($180°$) are equal.
Subtract $\angle DOB$ from both sides: $\angle AOD = \angle COB$. ∎

cards.answer: Vertically opposite angles are equal (a direct proof).

cards.title: Worked example: a two-column proof
cards.problem: Prove that the angles of a triangle add up to 180°.

steps.text: Given: triangle ABC. Construction: draw the line through A parallel to BC; mark angles x (left) and y (right) next to ∠A on this line.
1. x = ∠B (alternate angles, parallel lines).
2. y = ∠C (alternate angles, parallel lines).
3. x + ∠A + y = 180° (angles on a straight line).
4. Substitute 1 and 2 into 3: ∠B + ∠A + ∠C = 180°. ∎

cards.title: Proof: the exterior angle theorem
cards.problem: Side $AC$ of triangle $ABC$ is extended past $C$. Prove that the exterior angle $x$ at $C$ equals $b + c$, the two opposite interior angles.

steps.text: $a + b + c = 180°$ — angle sum of a triangle.
$x + a = 180°$ — $x$ and $a$ form a straight angle.
So $x + a = a + b + c$ (both equal $180°$).
Subtract $a$: $x = b + c$. ∎

cards.title: Proof: the sum of two odd numbers is even
cards.problem: Prove that the sum of any two odd integers is even.

steps.text: An even number has the form $2k$; an odd number has the form $2k + 1$ ($k$ an integer).
Let the odd numbers be $x = 2m + 1$ and $y = 2n + 1$.
$m + n + 1$ is an integer, so $x + y$ is 2 times an integer: even. ∎ (Checking $3 + 5 = 8$ only verifies one case.)

cards.title: Worked example: find the error in a "proof" that 2 = 1
cards.problem: Let $a = b$. Then $a^2 = ab$, $a^2 - b^2 = ab - b^2$, $(a - b)(a + b) = b(a - b)$, so $a + b = b$, $2b = b$ and $2 = 1$. What is wrong?

steps.text: Every step is fine up to $(a - b)(a + b) = b(a - b)$.
The next step divides both sides by $a - b$.
But $a = b$, so $a - b = 0$: the "proof" **divides by zero**, which is not allowed.
Lesson: each step of a proof needs a valid reason — check especially divisions and square roots.

cards.title: Inductive reasoning with polygons
body: From one vertex, an $n$-sided polygon has $n - 3$ diagonals, which cut it into $n - 2$ triangles. So the angle sum is $(n - 2) \times 180°$ — this conjecture is proved in Unit 3.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand how to form a converse**
A conditional statement is in the form "If $$P$$, then $$Q$$." Its converse is formed by interchanging the hypothesis ($$P$$) and the conclusion ($$Q$$), resulting in "If $$Q$$, then $$P$$."

**Step 2: Identify $$P$$ and $$Q$$**
- $$P$$ (Hypothesis): "a triangle is isosceles"
- $$Q$$ (Conclusion): "two of its sides are equal"

**Step 3: Swap $$P$$ and $$Q$$**
The converse is: "If two sides of a triangle are equal, then the triangle is isosceles."

**Step 4: Final Result**
The converse statement is **If two sides of a triangle are equal, then the triangle is isosceles.**

questions.q: How many lines can be drawn through two different points? Through three collinear points? Through three non-collinear points (taking two at a time)?
why: Step 1: postulate P2 — two points determine exactly one line.
Step 2: three collinear points all lie on that one line.
Step 3: three non-collinear points give 3 pairs → 3 different lines (the sides of a triangle).
questions.tip: Count pairs: $n$ points, no three collinear, give $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ lines.

similar.q: How many lines are determined by 4 points, no three collinear?

questions.label: 2.1 Practice — axiomatic systems

questions.q: Two rays lie on the same line, have a common end point and no other common points. What angle do they form?
why: Step 1: the rays point in opposite directions from the common end point.
Step 2: together they make a straight line.
Step 3: a straight angle measures $180°$.
questions.tip: Opposite rays always form a straight angle.

similar.q: Two rays from one point form a right angle. What is its measure?

questions.label: 2.1 Practice — axiomatic systems

questions.q: Why is "a line is a set of points" not a good definition?
questions.answer: It does not say which points; a circle or a triangle is also a set of points.
why: Step 1: a definition must pick out exactly one kind of object.
Step 2: many figures are sets of points.
Step 3: so the sentence is true about lines but does not define them.
questions.tip: Test a definition by looking for something else that fits it.

similar.q: Is "a square is a quadrilateral with four equal sides" a complete definition?
similar.a: No — a rhombus also fits; add "and four right angles".

questions.label: 2.1 Practice — axiomatic systems

questions.q: Which statement is a postulate about planes?

options.B: If two planes intersect, their intersection is a line
options.C: A plane contains only two points

why: Step 1: planes have no edges (A false).
Step 2: a plane contains at least three non-collinear points (C false).
Step 3: parallel planes never meet (D false). B is postulate P4.
questions.tip: Picture two walls of a room: they meet along a line.

similar.q: Where do the floor and a wall of a room meet?
similar.a: Along a line (the bottom edge of the wall).

questions.label: 2.1 Practice — axiomatic systems

questions.q: In the construction that copies a segment $PQ$ to $RS$, why is $RS = PQ$?

options.A: Because we measured both with a ruler
options.B: Because both are radii of the same compass setting
options.C: Because $R$ and $P$ are the same point
options.D: Because the arc is a straight line

why: Step 1: the compass was opened to $PQ$.
Step 2: the same width drew the arc from $R$.
Step 3: every point of that arc is $PQ$ away from $R$ — so $RS = PQ$.
questions.tip: In constructions, equal compass widths = equal lengths.

similar.q: When bisecting a segment, why must both pairs of arcs use the same width?
similar.a: So that the crossing points are equally far from both ends (they lie on the perpendicular bisector).

questions.label: 2.2 Practice — constructions and inscribed polygons

questions.q: After bisecting a 6 cm segment $AB$ with arcs, you join the arc crossings $P$ and $Q$. Give two facts about line $PQ$.
questions.answer: $PQ$ passes through the midpoint $M$ of $AB$ ($AM = MB = 3$ cm), and $PQ \perp AB$.
why: Step 1: $P$ and $Q$ are each the same distance from $A$ and $B$.
Step 2: all such points lie on the perpendicular bisector.
Step 3: so $PQ$ cuts $AB$ in half at right angles.
questions.tip: Perpendicular bisector = "cuts in half" + "at 90°".

similar.q: A 7 cm segment is bisected. How long is each half?

questions.label: 2.2 Practice — constructions and inscribed polygons

questions.q: An angle of $70°$ is bisected, and then one of the halves is bisected again. What is the size of the smallest angle?
why: Step 1: bisecting halves the angle: $70° \div 2 = 35°$.
Step 2: bisecting again: $35° \div 2 = 17.5°$.
questions.tip: Each bisection divides by 2: after $k$ bisections the angle is $\frac{\theta}{2^k}$.

similar.q: How can you construct a $45°$ angle with compass and straightedge?
similar.a: Construct a $90°$ angle (perpendicular bisector) and bisect it.

questions.label: 2.2 Practice — constructions and inscribed polygons

questions.q: A rectangle with sides 8 and 6 units is inscribed in a circle. Find the radius and say where the centre is.
questions.answer: Radius 5 units; the centre is where the diagonals cross.
why: Step 1: a diagonal of an inscribed rectangle is a diameter.
Step 2: diagonal $= \sqrt{8^2 + 6^2} = 10$.
Step 3: radius $= 10 \div 2 = 5$; the diagonals meet at the centre.
questions.tip: Inscribed rectangle → diagonal = diameter (the right angle stands on a diameter).

similar.q: A rectangle 12 × 5 is inscribed in a circle. Find the radius.

questions.label: 2.2 Practice — constructions and inscribed polygons

questions.q: To construct a regular octagon inscribed in a circle, the angle at the centre between neighbouring vertices is
why: Step 1: the full turn is $360°$.
Step 2: 8 equal parts: $360° \div 8 = 45°$.
questions.tip: Central angle of a regular $n$-gon $= \frac{360°}{n}$.

similar.q: What is the central angle for a regular pentagon?

questions.label: 2.2 Practice — constructions and inscribed polygons

questions.q: A regular hexagon is inscribed in a circle of radius 4 cm. Find its perimeter.
why: Step 1: central angle $= 60°$ and the two radii are equal, so each central triangle is equilateral.
Step 2: so each side $= $ radius $= 4$ cm.
Step 3: perimeter $= 6 \times 4 = 24$ cm.
questions.tip: Hexagon side = radius — the compass never needs re-setting.

similar.q: A regular hexagon has perimeter 30 cm. What is the radius of its circumscribed circle?

questions.label: 2.2 Practice — constructions and inscribed polygons

questions.q: $AB = 4$ cm and $CD = 1.5$ cm. Which length do you get by laying $AB$, $AB$ and $CD$ end to end? And $AB - CD$?
why: Step 1: end to end means add: $4 + 4 + 1.5 = 9.5$.
Step 2: for a difference, copy $AB$ then cut $CD$ back from its end: $4 - 1.5 = 2.5$.
questions.tip: Adding segments: lay them in the same direction; subtracting: lay the second one backwards from the end.

similar.q: Construct $3CD$ if $CD = 2$ cm. How long is it?

questions.label: 2.2 Practice — constructions and inscribed polygons

questions.q: Which is a counter-example to "every prime number is odd"?
why: Step 1: a counter-example must be prime AND not odd.
Step 2: 2 is prime and even.
Step 3: 9 and 15 are not prime; 3 is odd.
questions.tip: A counter-example must satisfy the hypothesis but break the conclusion.

similar.q: Give a counter-example to "every quadrilateral with 4 equal sides is a square".
similar.a: A rhombus that is not a square.

questions.label: 2.3 Practice — conjectures and counter-examples

questions.q: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One alternate interior angle is $65°$. Find the other alternate interior angle and the co-interior angle next to it.
why: Step 1: alternate interior angles are equal: $65°$.
Step 2: co-interior angles add up to $180°$: $180° - 65° = 115°$.
questions.tip: Z → equal, F → equal, C → add to $180°$.

similar.q: A corresponding angle is $112°$. Find its co-interior partner.

questions.label: 2.3 Practice — conjectures and counter-examples

questions.q: Two lines intersect. One angle is $3x + 10°$ and the vertically opposite angle is $5x - 30°$. Find $x$ and all four angles.
why: Step 1: vertically opposite angles are equal: $3x + 10 = 5x - 30$.
Step 2: $40 = 2x \Rightarrow x = 20$.
questions.tip: Vertically opposite → set equal. Neighbours on a line → add to $180°$.

similar.q: Vertically opposite angles are $2x$ and $x + 40$. Find $x$.

questions.label: 2.3 Practice — conjectures and counter-examples

questions.q: Conjecture: the number of regions when $n$ lines pass through the centre of a circle. How many regions do 6 lines give?
why: Step 2: each line adds 2.
Step 3: $2 \times 6 = 12$.
questions.tip: Look at the differences in a table — a constant difference $d$ means the rule is $dn + c$.
questions.label: 2.3 Practice — conjectures and counter-examples

questions.q: If a conjecture is true for 100 examples, it is proved.
why: Step 1: examples only verify particular cases.
Step 2: the 101st case could fail (like the circle-regions pattern that breaks at 6 points).
Step 3: only a general deductive argument proves it.
questions.tip: Examples can disprove (one counter-example) but cannot prove.

similar.q: How many counter-examples are needed to disprove a conjecture?

questions.label: 2.3 Practice — conjectures and counter-examples

questions.q: Make a conjecture about (a) the diagonals of a rectangle, (b) the base angles of an isosceles triangle.
questions.answer: (a) They are equal and bisect each other. (b) They are equal.
why: Step 1: draw several rectangles; measure the diagonals — always equal, crossing at their midpoints.
Step 2: draw isosceles triangles; measure the angles opposite the equal sides — always equal.
questions.tip: Draw at least three different-looking cases before you state a conjecture.

similar.q: Conjecture about the diagonals of a rhombus?
similar.a: They bisect each other at right angles.

questions.label: 2.3 Practice — conjectures and counter-examples

questions.q: Make a correct deduction: "All rectangles are parallelograms. $ABCD$ is a rectangle."
why: Step 1: general statement: rectangle ⇒ parallelogram.
Step 2: particular case: $ABCD$ is a rectangle.
Step 3: so $ABCD$ is a parallelogram (deductive reasoning).
questions.tip: Pattern: If $p$ then $q$; $p$; therefore $q$.

similar.q: "All human beings are mortal. Socrates is a human being." Conclusion?

questions.label: 2.4 Practice — reasoning and proof

questions.q: Angles $A$ and $B$ are complementary and $\angle A = x°$. What can you deduce about $\angle B$?
why: Step 1: complementary means $\angle A + \angle B = 90°$.
Step 2: $\angle B = 90° - x°$.
questions.tip: Complementary → 90° (Corner), supplementary → 180° (Straight).

similar.q: $\angle P$ and $\angle Q$ are supplementary, $\angle P = 3x$. Find $\angle Q$.

questions.label: 2.4 Practice — reasoning and proof

questions.q: The converse of "If a triangle is isosceles, then two of its sides are equal" is

options.A: If two sides of a triangle are equal, then it is isosceles
options.B: If a triangle is not isosceles, then no two sides are equal
options.D: If a figure is a triangle then it is isosceles

why: Step 1: hypothesis $p$ = "a triangle is isosceles"; conclusion $q$ = "two sides are equal".
Step 2: converse = "if $q$ then $p$".
questions.tip: Converse = swap the "if" part and the "then" part.

similar.q: Converse of "If the radius is 5, the area is $25\pi$"?
similar.a: If the area is $25\pi$, then the radius is 5.

questions.label: 2.4 Practice — reasoning and proof

questions.q: Write the hypothesis, conclusion and converse of "If opposite sides of a quadrilateral are parallel, then it is a parallelogram." Is the converse true?
questions.answer: Hypothesis: opposite sides parallel. Conclusion: it is a parallelogram. Converse: if a quadrilateral is a parallelogram, then its opposite sides are parallel — true.
why: Step 1: the "if" part is the hypothesis.
Step 2: the "then" part is the conclusion.
Step 3: swap them for the converse; it is true by the definition of a parallelogram.
questions.tip: Definitions are always "if and only if", so their converses are true.

similar.q: Is the converse of "If a figure is a square, then it is a rectangle" true?
similar.a: No — a 4 × 2 rectangle is not a square.

questions.label: 2.4 Practice — reasoning and proof

questions.q: In triangle $ABC$, $\angle A = 48°$ and $\angle B = 67°$. Side $AC$ is extended beyond $C$. Find the exterior angle at $C$ in two ways.
why: Way 1 (exterior angle theorem): $48° + 67° = 115°$.
questions.tip: The exterior angle theorem saves a step: just add the two far angles.

similar.q: An exterior angle of a triangle is $130°$ and one remote interior angle is $55°$. Find the other.

questions.label: 2.4 Practice — reasoning and proof

questions.q: Prove: the sum of two even integers is even.
why: Step 1: let the even integers be $2m$ and $2n$ ($m, n$ integers).
Step 2: add: $2m + 2n = 2(m + n)$.
Step 3: $m + n$ is an integer, so the sum is even. ∎
questions.tip: Write general even/odd numbers with letters: even $2k$, odd $2k + 1$.

similar.q: Prove that the product of two odd integers is odd.

questions.label: 2.4 Practice — reasoning and proof

questions.q: Reasoning from several particular cases to a general rule is called ____ reasoning.
why: Step 1: particular → general = inductive.
Step 2: general → particular = deductive.
questions.tip: IN-ductive: cases come IN, a rule comes out.

similar.q: Reasoning that uses axioms and theorems to reach a certain conclusion is called ____.

questions.label: 2.4 Practice — reasoning and proof

questions.q: Use the polygon table to find (a) the number of triangles and (b) the angle sum of a decagon (10 sides).
why: Step 1: triangles from one vertex $= n - 2 = 8$.
Step 2: each triangle has $180°$.
questions.tip: Angle sum $= (n - 2) \times 180°$.

similar.q: How many diagonals can be drawn from one vertex of a 12-gon?

lessons.title: Angle and Side Properties of Polygons

cards.title: 3.1.1 Polygons and their names
body: A **polygon** is a closed plane figure made of straight line segments (its **sides**) such that each side meets exactly two others, at its end points (the **vertices**), and the sides do not cross each other. A figure with a curved side, a gap, or two sides crossing in the middle is **not** a polygon.
Polygons are named by the number of sides $n$: 3 triangle, 4 quadrilateral, 5 pentagon, 6 hexagon, 7 heptagon, 8 octagon, 9 nonagon, 10 decagon, 12 dodecagon; in general an **$n$-gon**.

A **regular polygon** is both **equilateral** (all sides equal) and **equiangular** (all angles equal). Both conditions are needed: a rhombus is equilateral but not equiangular; a rectangle is equiangular but not equilateral; only the square is regular. (For triangles alone, equilateral already forces equiangular.)

cards.title: Only the first figure is a polygon
Regular polygons: equal sides AND equal angles
3.1.2 Sum of the interior angles
body: **Theorem 3.1 — triangle:** the three angles of any triangle add up to $180°$. Proof idea: draw the line through $A$ parallel to $BC$. The two alternate angles at $A$ equal $b$ and $c$, and together with $a$ they make a straight angle, so $a + b + c = 180°$.
**Any polygon:** from one vertex of an $n$-gon draw all the diagonals. They cut it into $(n - 2)$ triangles, and the angles of these triangles make up exactly the interior angles of the polygon. So:
For a **regular** $n$-gon all $n$ angles are equal, so each interior angle is $\dfrac{(n - 2) \times 180°}{n}$.
Working backwards: if you know the angle sum $S$, then $n - 2 = \frac{S}{180°}$, so $n = \frac{S}{180°} + 2$. If this is not a whole number, no such polygon exists.

cards.title: Worked example: missing angles in triangles
cards.problem: (a) A triangle has angles $x$, $30°$ and $130°$. (b) An isosceles triangle has two equal angles $x$ and a third angle $70°$. Find $x$.

steps.text: (b) $x + x + 70° = 180° \Rightarrow 2x = 110° \Rightarrow x = 55°$.

cards.title: Worked example: using the angle-sum formula both ways
cards.problem: (a) Find each interior angle of a regular 12-gon. (b) A polygon has interior angle sum $2160°$. How many sides? (c) Six angles of a heptagon add up to $820°$; find the seventh.

steps.text: (b) $(n - 2) \times 180° = 2160° \Rightarrow n - 2 = 12 \Rightarrow n = 14$ sides.
(c) Heptagon: $S = 5 \times 180° = 900°$; seventh angle $= 900° - 820° = 80°$.

steps.text: **Step 1: Write down the interior angle sum formula**

cards.title: 3.1.3 Exterior angle of a triangle
body: Extend one side of a triangle. The angle between the extension and the next side is an **exterior angle**. The two angles of the triangle that are **not** next to it are its **opposite (remote) interior angles**.
**Theorem 3.2 (exterior angle theorem):** an exterior angle of a triangle equals the **sum of the two opposite interior angles**.
Proof: $a + b + c = 180°$ (angle sum) and $c + d = 180°$ (straight line), so $a + b + c = c + d$, hence $d = a + b$.
Consequence: an exterior angle is always **bigger than each** opposite interior angle.

cards.title: Worked example: exterior angle theorem
cards.problem: In triangle $ABC$, the exterior angle at $C$ is $110°$ and $\angle A = 60°$. Find the interior angle $a$ at $C$ and the angle $b$ at $B$. Then find the exterior angle at $B$.

steps.text: Interior and exterior at $C$ lie on a straight line: $a = 180° - 110° = 70°$.
Exterior angle theorem at $C$: $110° = \angle A + \angle B = 60° + b$, so $b = 50°$.
Exterior angle at $B$ $= \angle A + \angle C = 60° + 70° = 130°$ (check: $180° - 50° = 130°$, correct).

cards.title: 3.1.4 Sum of the exterior angles of a polygon
body: At each vertex take **one** exterior angle (extend the sides in turn, all in the same direction round the polygon).
**Theorem 3.4:** the exterior angles of **any** polygon add up to $360°$ — whatever the number of sides.

Proof: at each of the $n$ vertices, interior + exterior $= 180°$, so all of them together give $n \times 180°$. The interior angles use $(n - 2) \times 180°$, so the exterior angles get $n \times 180° - (n - 2) \times 180° = 2 \times 180° = 360°$.
Picture: walk round the polygon; at each corner you turn through the exterior angle; after one lap you face the starting direction again — one full turn, $360°$.

For a **regular** $n$-gon: each exterior angle $= \dfrac{360°}{n}$, so $n = \dfrac{360°}{\text{exterior angle}}$. This is the **fastest** way to find $n$ from an interior angle: exterior $= 180° -$ interior.

cards.title: Worked example: regular polygons from their angles
cards.problem: (a) Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is $60°$. How many sides? (b) Each interior angle is $156°$. How many sides? (c) Is there a regular polygon with interior angle $100°$?

steps.text: (a) $n = 360° \div 60° = 6$ (hexagon).
(c) Exterior $= 80°$, $360° \div 80° = 4.5$ — not a whole number, so **no** such regular polygon.

cards.title: Tip: go through the exterior angle
body: Interior angle given → subtract from $180°$ → divide $360°$ by it. Example: $140°$ → $40°$ → $n = 9$. Much quicker than solving $\frac{(n-2)180}{n} = 140$.

cards.title: Geometric patterns
body: (n−2)×180° = sum of interior angles of an n-gon
Each exterior of a triangle is equal to the sum of the two interior opposites. Sum of one exterior at each vertex of any convex polygon = 360°.

cards.title: More notes
body: Always name the arc when you claim “angle at the centre is twice…”. Wrong arc is the standard error. For polygons, interior + adjacent exterior = 180° if the exterior is the extension of one side.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the sum of the interior angles of a 15-sided polygon?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Write down the interior angle sum formula**
The sum of the interior angles $$S$$ of an $$n$$-sided polygon is:
$$S = (n - 2) \times 180^{\circ}$$

**Step 2: Substitute $$n = 15$$ into the formula**
$$S = (15 - 2) \times 180^{\circ}$$
$$S = 13 \times 180^{\circ}$$

**Step 3: Perform the multiplication**
$$S = 2340^{\circ}$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The sum of the interior angles is **$$2340^{\circ}$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Calculate the measure of each interior angle of a regular octagon.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Write down the formula for one interior angle**
For a regular polygon with $$n$$ sides, each interior angle is:
$$\text{Angle} = \frac{(n - 2) \times 180^{\circ}}{n}$$

**Step 2: Substitute $$n = 8$$ for an octagon**
$$\text{Angle} = \frac{(8 - 2) \times 180^{\circ}}{8}$$
$$\text{Angle} = \frac{6 \times 180^{\circ}}{8}$$
$$\text{Angle} = \frac{1080^{\circ}}{8}$$

**Step 3: Simplify the fraction**
$$\text{Angle} = 135^{\circ}$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
Each interior angle of a regular octagon is **$$135^{\circ}$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If the sum of the interior angles of a polygon is $$2160^{\circ}$$, how many sides does the polygon have?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Set up the equation using the sum formula**
$$(n - 2) \times 180^{\circ} = 2160^{\circ}$$

**Step 2: Solve for $$(n - 2)$$**
Divide both sides by $$180^{\circ}$$:
$$n - 2 = \frac{2160}{180}$$
$$n - 2 = 12$$

**Step 3: Solve for $$n$$**
$$n = 12 + 2$$
$$n = 14$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The polygon has **$$14$$** sides.

lessons.title: Angles and Arc Relationship of Circles

cards.title: 3.2.1 Parts of a circle, central and inscribed angles
body: A **chord** joins two points of the circle. A chord through the centre is a **diameter** (the longest chord, $d = 2r$). A **radius** joins the centre to the circle. An **arc** is a part of the circle: a **minor arc** is less than half the circle, a **major arc** more than half, a **semicircle** exactly half.
The **measure of an arc** is the measure of the central angle that stands on it (a full circle is $360°$).
- A **central angle** has its vertex at the centre $O$.
- An **inscribed angle** has its vertex **on the circle** and its arms are chords.
**Theorem 3.5 (inscribed angle theorem):** an inscribed angle is **half** the central angle standing on the same arc: $\angle ABC = \frac12 \angle AOC = \frac12 m(\text{arc } AC)$.
Two very useful consequences:
- **Angle in a semicircle** is a right angle ($90°$): the central angle on a diameter is $180°$.
- **Angles on the same arc are equal**: they are all half of the same central angle.

cards.title: Inscribed angle = half of the central angle
body: Both angles stand on the red arc $AC$. If $\angle ABC = 70°$ then $\angle AOC = 140°$ and arc $AC$ measures $140°$.

cards.title: Proof of the inscribed angle theorem (centre on one arm)
cards.problem: Let $O$ lie on $BC$. Prove $\angle ABC = \frac12\angle AOC$.

steps.text: Draw $OA$. $OA = OB$ (radii), so triangle $AOB$ is isosceles and $\angle OAB = \angle ABC$.
$\angle AOC$ is an exterior angle of triangle $AOB$, so $\angle AOC = \angle OAB + \angle ABC = 2\angle ABC$.
Divide by 2: $\angle ABC = \frac12\angle AOC$. ∎ (Other positions of $O$ follow by adding or subtracting two such cases.)

cards.title: Angle in a semicircle; angles on the same arc
Worked example: central and inscribed angles
cards.problem: (a) An inscribed angle $\angle B = 70°$ stands on arc $ADC$. Find the arc. (b) Arc $DBF$ measures $130°$; find the inscribed angle $\angle DKF$ on it. (c) $AB$ is a diameter and $\angle CAB = 35°$; find $\angle ABC$.

steps.text: (b) $\angle DKF = \frac12 \times 130° = 65°$.
(c) $\angle ACB = 90°$ (semicircle), so $\angle ABC = 180° - 90° - 35° = 55°$.

cards.title: 3.2.2 Cyclic quadrilaterals
body: A quadrilateral whose four vertices lie on a circle is a **cyclic quadrilateral**.
**Theorem 3.6:** the **opposite angles** of a cyclic quadrilateral are **supplementary** (add up to $180°$).

Proof: $\angle A$ stands on arc $BCD$ and $\angle C$ on arc $BAD$; the two arcs make the whole circle. So $\angle A + \angle C = \frac12(\text{arc } BCD + \text{arc } BAD) = \frac12 \times 360° = 180°$.
Consequence: an exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior **opposite** angle.
Converse (useful test): if a pair of opposite angles of a quadrilateral add up to $180°$, its vertices lie on a circle.

cards.title: Worked example: cyclic quadrilateral
cards.problem: In cyclic quadrilateral $JKLM$, $\angle L = 96°$ and $\angle K = 80°$. Find $\angle J$ and $\angle M$.

steps.text: $J$ and $L$ are opposite: $\angle J = 180° - 96° = 84°$.
$K$ and $M$ are opposite: $\angle M = 180° - 80° = 100°$.
Check: $84° + 80° + 96° + 100° = 360°$ (correct) (angle sum of a quadrilateral).

cards.title: Worked example: angles in a circle
cards.problem: O is the centre of a circle. A, B, C, D lie on the circle with ABCD a cyclic quadrilateral. The central angle on the minor arc AC is ∠AOC = 140°, B lies on the major arc and D on the minor arc. Find ∠ABC and ∠ADC.

steps.text: Step 1: the angle at the circumference on the same arc is half the central angle. If B is on the major arc, ∠ABC = ½ × 140° = 70°.
Step 2: ABCD is cyclic, so opposite angles are supplementary: ∠ADC = 180° − 70° = 110°.
Step 3: check: D is on the minor arc, and its angle uses the reflex central angle 360° − 140° = 220°, half of which is 110° ✔.

cards.title: Angle between two chords crossing inside
body: **Theorem 3.7:** when two chords cross inside a circle, each angle at the crossing point is **half the sum** of the arc it faces and the arc its vertically opposite angle faces:
$$x = \tfrac12(\text{arc } AB + \text{arc } CD)$$
Proof: join $B$ to $C$. $x$ is an exterior angle of the small triangle, so it equals the sum of two inscribed angles, which are half of the two arcs.

cards.title: Worked example: chords crossing inside
cards.problem: Two chords cross inside a circle. The arcs facing the angle $a$ and its opposite angle measure $35°$ and $65°$. Find $a$.

steps.text: Use $a = \frac12(\text{sum of the two arcs})$.

cards.title: 3.2.3 Tangents
body: A **tangent** is a line that touches the circle at exactly **one** point, the **point of contact (tangency)**. A **secant** is a line that cuts the circle at two points.
- **Tangent is perpendicular to the radius:** the tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.
- **Two tangents from one external point are equal**: $PA = PB$, and $OP$ bisects the angle $APB$. In quadrilateral $PAOB$ the two right angles give $\angle APB + \angle AOB = 180°$.

- **Tangent–chord angle (Theorem 3.8):** the angle between a tangent and a chord at the point of contact equals the inscribed angle on the **opposite** side of the chord (in the "alternate segment"). It is half the arc cut off by the chord.
- **Parallel chords** cut off equal arcs between them.

cards.title: Tangent is perpendicular to the radius
Angle in the alternate segment
body: The angle $x$ between tangent $PB$ and chord $PS$ equals the angle $PTS$ at any point $T$ on the arc on the other side of $PS$.

cards.title: Angle formed outside the circle
body: **Theorem 3.9:** if two secants (or a secant and a tangent, or two tangents) meet at a point $P$ **outside** the circle, the angle at $P$ is **half the difference** of the two arcs they cut off:
$$\angle P = \tfrac12(\text{far arc} - \text{near arc})$$
Compare: inside → half the **sum**; on the circle → **half** the arc; outside → half the **difference**.

cards.title: Worked example: angle outside the circle
cards.problem: Two secants from $Q$ cut off arcs $PTR = 120°$ (far) and $SLM$ (near). If $\angle PQR = 36°$, find arc $SLM$.

steps.text: $\angle Q = \frac12(\text{far} - \text{near})$: $36° = \frac12(120° - x)$.
$72° = 120° - x \Rightarrow x = 48°$.

cards.title: Worked example: two tangents
cards.problem: Two tangents from an external point make an angle of $80°$. Find the two arcs between the points of contact.

steps.text: Let the minor arc be $x$; the major arc is $360° - x$.
Outside angle: $80° = \frac12((360° - x) - x) = 180° - x$.
So $x = 100°$ and the major arc is $260°$. (Also: $\angle AOB = 180° - 80° = 100°$.)

cards.title: Angles and Arc Relationship of Circles
body: Circle: angle in a semicircle = 90°. Angle at the centre = twice the angle at the circumference on the same arc. Angles in the same segment are equal. Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°. Tangent ⊥ radius. Two tangents from an external point are equal.

cards.title: 3.3 Lengths of chords, secants and tangents
body: Three "product" theorems connect the lengths of segments cut off by a circle. Each says: **(part × part) on one line = (part × part) on the other line**, where all the parts are measured **from the crossing point**.

cards.title: 3.3.1 Two chords crossing inside
body: If chords $RS$ and $TQ$ cross at $E$ inside the circle, then
$$RE \times ES = TE \times EQ$$
Reason: triangles $RET$ and $QES$ are similar (equal angles on the same arcs and vertically opposite angles), so $\frac{RE}{TE} = \frac{EQ}{ES}$.

cards.title: Worked example: intersecting chords
cards.problem: Chords $RS$ and $TQ$ cross at $E$. $RE = 7$, $ES = 8$ and $EQ = 4$. Find $TE$.

steps.text: $RE \times ES = TE \times EQ$.
$7 \times 8 = TE \times 4$.

cards.title: Worked example: intersecting chords
cards.problem: Chords AB and CD meet at E inside a circle. AE = 6 cm, EB = 4 cm and CE = 3 cm. Find ED and the length of CD.

steps.text: Step 1: intersecting chords theorem: AE × EB = CE × ED.
Step 2: 6 × 4 = 3 × ED → 24 = 3·ED → ED = 8 cm.
Step 3: CD = CE + ED = 3 + 8 = 11 cm.

cards.title: 3.3.2 A tangent and a secant from one point
body: From an external point $P$ draw a tangent touching at $A$ and a secant cutting the circle at $B$ (near) and $C$ (far). Then
$$PA^2 = PB \times PC$$
The tangent is "its own two parts" (both from $P$ to $A$), so it appears squared. **$PC$ is the whole secant**, not just the part inside the circle.

cards.title: Worked example: tangent and secant
cards.problem: Tangent $PA = 12$. A secant from $P$ has outside part $PB = 6$ and inside part $BC = x$. Find $x$.

steps.text: $PA^2 = PB \times PC$ with $PC = 6 + x$.
$6x = 108 \Rightarrow x = 18$.

cards.title: 3.3.3 Two secants from one point
body: If two secants from an external point $P$ cut the circle at $A, B$ and at $C, D$ ($A$, $C$ nearer to $P$), then
$$PA \times PB = PC \times PD$$
"**Outside part × whole secant** is the same for both secants." Proof: both products equal $PE^2$ for a tangent $PE$ from $P$.

cards.title: Worked example: two secants
cards.problem: $PA = 6$, $AB = 6$ and $PC = 4$. Find $CD = x$.

steps.text: Whole secants: $PB = 6 + 6 = 12$ and $PD = 4 + x$.
$PA \times PB = PC \times PD$: $6 \times 12 = 4(4 + x)$.
$72 = 16 + 4x \Rightarrow 4x = 56 \Rightarrow x = 14$.

cards.title: Worked example: an equation from crossing chords
cards.problem: Chords $PQ$ and $RS$ cross at $A$. $PA = 12$, $QA = x$, $RA = x + 1$ and $SA = x + 6$. Find $PQ$ and $RS$.

steps.text: $PA \cdot QA = RA \cdot SA$: $12x = (x + 1)(x + 6) = x^2 + 7x + 6$.

cards.why: Tangent–secant theorem: PT² = PA × PB → 64 = 4 × PB → PB = 16 cm.

cards.why: PA × PB = PC × PD → 3 × 12 = 4 × PD → PD = 9.

cards.title: 4.1.1 Polyhedrons
body: Plane figures have length and width and therefore they are called **two-dimensional figures**.
A solid object has length, width, and height.
**A solid** is an enclosed portion of space bounded by plane or curved surfaces.
**A polyhedron** is a solid bounded by plane (flat) surfaces only.

cards.title: 4.1.2 Cylinders, Cones and Spheres
body: **A circular cone** is a solid whose base is a circle and whose lateral surface come to a point.

If a plane parallel to the base intersects a cone, not at the vertex, the part of the cone bounded by the base, the cross-section, and the portion of the lateral surface between the plane is called a **frustum of the cone**.
A sphere is formed by revolving a semicircle about its diameter as an axis.
The outer end of the radius perpendicular to the axis generates a great circle while the outer ends of the other chords perpendicular to the diameter generate small circles.

cards.title: 4.1.3 Nets and Views of Solids
body: A **net** is a flat pattern that folds up into a solid. A cube has 6 square faces, so every net of a cube is made of 6 squares joined edge to edge — there are 11 different cube nets (for example a "cross" of 4 squares in a row with one square above and one below the second square). A regular tetrahedron has 4 equilateral-triangle faces; its common net is one large triangle divided into 4 smaller triangles.

Solids are also drawn by their **views**: the **front view**, **side view** and **top view (plan)**. A cylinder standing upright has a rectangle as front view and a circle as top view; a square pyramid has a triangle as front view and a square with its diagonals as top view.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Verify Euler's Formula for a triangular prism ($$F = 5$$, $$V = 6$$, and $$E = 9$$). What is the value of $$F + V - E$$?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify the variables**
For a triangular prism, we are given:
- Faces ($$F$$) = $$5$$
- Vertices ($$V$$) = $$6$$
- Edges ($$E$$) = $$9$$

**Step 2: Substitute the values into Euler's Formula**
The expression is $$F + V - E$$:
$$5 + 6 - 9$$

**Step 3: Simplify the expression**
$$11 - 9 = 2$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The value is **$$2$$**, which confirms Euler's Formula.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following three-dimensional solids is NOT a polyhedron?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Recall the definition of a polyhedron**
A polyhedron is a three-dimensional solid bounded strictly by flat, polygonal plane surfaces.

**Step 2: Analyze the geometric shapes**
- Triangular prisms, square pyramids, and regular tetrahedrons are all bounded strictly by flat polygons (triangles, squares, rectangles). Thus, they are polyhedrons.
- A cylinder has a curved lateral surface and circular bases, which are not polygons. Thus, it is not a polyhedron.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The curved solid that is not a polyhedron is **A cylinder**.

**Step 2:** Check with Euler's formula: F + V − E = 6 + 8 − 12 = 2.

**Step 3:** Answer: 6, 12, 8.

**Tip:** Euler's formula F + V − E = 2 holds for every convex polyhedron – use it to check counts.

cards.title: 4.2.1 Coordinates in a Plane
body: The **x-axis** and **y-axis** meet at the origin O(0, 0) and divide the plane into four **quadrants**: I (+, +), II (−, +), III (−, −), IV (+, −). In the pair (a, b), a is the x-coordinate (abscissa) and b the y-coordinate (ordinate).
**Distance formula:** $$PQ = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}$$ — Pythagoras on the grid. **Midpoint formula:** $$M = \left(\frac{x_1 + x_2}{2}, \frac{y_1 + y_2}{2}\right)$$.

**Example:** show that P(−2, 3), Q(3, 8), R(4, 1) form an isosceles triangle. PQ = √(5² + 5²) = √50; QR = √(1² + (−7)²) = √50; PR = √(6² + (−2)²) = √40. Two sides are equal (PQ = QR), so the triangle is isosceles.
**Collinear test:** three points are collinear if the two shorter distances add up to the longest one (or if the slopes between them are equal).

cards.title: Key formulas of coordinate geometry
body: **Distance** between $A(x_1, y_1)$ and $B(x_2, y_2)$: $AB = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}$.
**Midpoint** of $AB$: $M = \left(\frac{x_1 + x_2}{2}, \frac{y_1 + y_2}{2}\right)$.

**Slope** of $AB$: $m = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$ ($x_1 
e x_2$). Parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular lines have slopes whose product is $-1$.
Example: for $A(1, 2)$ and $B(4, 6)$, $AB = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$, the midpoint is $(2.5, 4)$ and the slope is $\frac{4}{3}$.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Write down the Distance Formula**
$$d = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}$$

**Step 2: Substitute coordinate values**
Here, $$(x_1, y_1) = (2, 4)$$ and $$(x_2, y_2) = (2, 10)$$:
$$d = \sqrt{(2 - 2)^2 + (10 - 4)^2}$$

$$d = \sqrt{36} = 6$$

cards.title: Transformations
body: Transformations: reflection (mirror line), translation (vector), dilation (centre + scale k). Distances: reflection and translation keep size (isometries). Dilation multiplies lengths by |k|; k<0 also turns through 180° about the centre in many school treatments.

cards.title: 4.3.1 Reflection
body: **A point** is the image of another point, across a line l, if the line l is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining the two points.
If the point lies on the line, the reflection is the point itself.
If C contains the reflection across L of each point of C, then C is symmetric about L.
The triangle ABC with vertices A(-3, 4), B(-2, 1), C(-6, -4) is reflected in the x-axis.

cards.title: 4.3.2 Translations
body: A translation moves every point the same distance in the same direction. i.e., a translation is a correspondence between points and their image points so that each image is the same distance in the same direction from the original point.
A translation takes every point a distance 1 to the left and 2 downward.

cards.title: 4.3.3 Dilation
body: When a shape is resized it gets bigger or smaller but it still looks similar that is, all angles stay the same and the relative sizes are the same.

cards.problem: Triangle ABC has A(1, 2), B(4, 2), C(1, 5). Translate it by (−3, 1), then reflect the image in the x-axis.

steps.text: Step 1: translate (add −3 to x and 1 to y): A′(−2, 3), B′(1, 3), C′(−2, 6).
Step 2: reflect in the x-axis (change the sign of y): A″(−2, −3), B″(1, −3), C″(−2, −6).
Step 3: both are isometries, so A″B″C″ is congruent to ABC (AB = 3 and A″B″ = 3 ✔).

units.intro:
Congruent figures: same shape and size — one maps onto the other by isometries. Triangle tests: SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS (right-angle, hypotenuse, side). AAA is similar, not congruent (Grade 11 similarity). AAS is ASA in disguise if you know the angle sum.

Corresponding vertices must be named in order. Tick sides and arcs on the diagram before you write a test name. Size also means perimeter and area recipes you already have — congruence says those match automatically.

**Step 1: Identify corresponding parts**

cards.q: A sector of a circle of radius $$6\text{ cm}$$ has a central angle of $$120^{\circ}$$. Find the area of the sector.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify the formula for the area of a sector**
The area $$A$$ of a sector with radius $$r$$ and central angle $$\theta$$ is:
$$A = \frac{\pi r^2 \theta}{360^{\circ}}$$

**Step 2: Substitute the known values**
Here, $$r = 6\text{ cm}$$ and $$\theta = 120^{\circ}$$:
$$A = \frac{\pi (6)^2 (120^{\circ})}{360^{\circ}}$$

**Step 3: Simplify the fractions**
Since $$\frac{120^{\circ}}{360^{\circ}} = \frac{1}{3}$$:
$$A = \pi \times 36 \times \frac{1}{3}$$
$$A = 12\pi\text{ cm}^2$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The area of the sector is **$$12\pi\text{ cm}^2$$**.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify the formula for an inscribed regular polygon**
The perimeter $$P$$ of a regular $$n$$-sided polygon inscribed in a circle of radius $$r$$ is:
$$P = 2nr \sin\left(\frac{180^{\circ}}{n}\right)$$

**Step 2: Substitute the known values**
Here, $$n = 10$$ and $$r = 5\text{ cm}$$. Therefore:
$$P = 2(10)(5) \sin\left(\frac{180^{\circ}}{10}\right)$$
$$P = 100 \sin(18^{\circ})$$

**Step 3: Calculate the numerical value**
Using the approximation $$\sin(18^{\circ}) \approx 0.3090$$:
$$P \approx 100 \times 0.3090 = 30.90\text{ cm}$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The perimeter of the decagon is **$$30.90\text{ cm}$$**.

cards.q: Find the area of a regular hexagon with a side length of $$4\text{ cm}$$.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify the formula for the area of a regular hexagon**
The area $$A$$ of a regular hexagon with side length $$s$$ is given by:
$$A = \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}s^2$$

**Step 2: Substitute $$s = 4\text{ cm}$$**

**Step 3: Simplify the expression**
$$A = 3\sqrt{3} \times 8$$
$$A = 24\sqrt{3}\text{ cm}^2$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The area of the regular hexagon is **$$24\sqrt{3}\text{ cm}^2$$**.

lessons.title: Surface Areas and Volumes of Solid Figures

cards.title: 5.3.1 Surface Areas and Volumes of Prisms
body: **Prism:** two congruent parallel bases joined by rectangular faces. Volume V = (area of base) × (height of the prism). Total surface area = 2 × (area of base) + (perimeter of base) × (height).

**Example — right triangular prism:** the bases are right-angled triangles with legs 3 cm and 4 cm (hypotenuse 5 cm), and the prism is 10 cm long. Base area = ½ × 3 × 4 = 6 cm². Volume = 6 × 10 = 60 cm³. Lateral area = (3 + 4 + 5) × 10 = 120 cm². Total surface area = 2 × 6 + 120 = 132 cm².

cards.title: 5.3.3 Surface Areas and Volumes of Pyramids

cards.title: 5.3.4 Surface Areas and Volumes of Cones

cards.title: 5.3.5 Surface Areas and Volumes of Spheres
body: The ancient Greeks knew the formulas for surface area and volume of a sphere.

Archimedes of Syracuse, a Greek mathematician who lived between 287 and 212 BCE, discovered that: The surface area of a sphere is the same as the lateral surface area of the smallest right cylinder containing the sphere.
A ball in the form of a sphere has a diameter of 14 cm long.
A basin has the shape of a hemisphere of diameter 42 centimetres.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify the formula for the volume of a sphere**
The volume $$V$$ of a sphere with radius $$r$$ is given by:
$$V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$$

$$V = 36\pi\text{ cm}^3$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The volume of the sphere is **$$36\pi\text{ cm}^3$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A right circular cylinder has a radius of $$7\text{ cm}$$ and a height of $$10\text{ cm}$$. Find its total surface area. (Take $$\pi = \frac{22}{7}$$)
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify the formula for total surface area of a cylinder**
The total surface area $$SA$$ of a cylinder is:
$$SA = 2\pi rh + 2\pi r^2 = 2\pi r(h + r)$$

**Step 2: Substitute the given values**
Here, $$r = 7\text{ cm}$$, $$h = 10\text{ cm}$$, and $$\pi = \frac{22}{7}$$:
$$SA = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 7 \times (10 + 7)$$

**Step 3: Simplify the expression**
$$SA = 24 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 7 \times 17$$
$$SA = 44 \times 17$$
$$SA = 748\text{ cm}^2$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The total surface area of the cylinder is **$$748\text{ cm}^2$$**.
